item.research_question: How does the application of a strong static magnetic field (SSMF) during solidification influence the microstructure evolution and the mechanical, electrical, and magnetic properties of FeCoNi(AlSi)0.2 high-entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Arc-melting under argon atmosphere followed by re-melting four times; samples vacuum-sealed in quartz tubes and solidified using a self-built 8-Tesla facility with heating rates of 0.3 °C/s to 1450 °C (held 1 h), cooling at 1 °C/s to ~1200 °C, and water quenching; magnetic field intensities applied at 0T, 1T, 3T, 5T, and 7T.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature compression tests (strain rate 5 × 10−4 s−1), Vickers hardness (200 g load, 15 s hold), four-probe resistivity measurement, and hysteresis loop testing via VSM at room temperature.
key_findings: Vickers hardness increases then decreases with magnetic field intensity, reaching a maximum of 190 HV (parallel) and 187 HV (perpendicular) at 5T.
Yield strength decreases then increases, reaching a minimum of 172 MPa at 5T.
Saturation magnetization (Ms) reaches a maximum of 121.7 emu/g (vertical) and 97.7 emu/g (parallel) at 5T.
Coercivity (Hc) reaches a minimum of 2.19 Oe (vertical) and 2.29 Oe (parallel) at 5T.
Electrical resistivity continuously increases with magnetic field intensity, reaching a maximum of 110 μΩ·cm at 7T.
A minor body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase precipitates in the perpendicular direction at 7T, while the alloy remains a single FCC phase up to 5T.
The volume fraction of dendritic phase is smallest at 5T, while the interdendritic phase volume fraction is largest at 5T.
item.mechanism: The magnetic field influences microstructure evolution (phase species, volume fraction, and crystal orientation), atomic-level structure, and defect density (vacancies and dislocations). The increase in resistivity is attributed to 'frozen' vacancies from quenching and increased dislocation density induced by the magnetic field. The variation in saturation magnetization is attributed to the magnetic field's effect on atomic-level structure, while coercivity changes are linked to grain size, grain boundary density, and the presence of the BCC phase at 7T.
item.limitations: The specific influence mechanism of the magnetic field on the atomic-level structure requires further study. The discontinuous change in resistivity and abnormal magnetic properties at 7T related to the precipitated BCC phase need verification by further experiments.
item.future_work: Further experiments are needed to verify the relationship between the precipitated BCC phase and the discontinuous changes in resistivity and magnetic properties at 7T, as well as to study the specific influence mechanism of the magnetic field on the atomic-level structure.
quotes: The main reasons for the magnetic field on the above effects are interpreted by microstructure evolution (phase species and volume fraction), atomic-level structure and defects (vacancy and dislocation density).
With the increasing magnetic field intensity, the resistivity has always been increased. Wang et al. found that the magnetic field can induce an increase of dislocation density [].
The discontinuous change at 7T may have some relation to the precipitated BCC phase. They still need to be verified by further experiments.
